title: Hamer v. Sidway
summary: Requested surrender of lawful freedom can supply consideration even when the promisee benefits from abstaining and the promisor receives no measurable economic gain.
notes:
Court: Court of Appeals of New York (1891).

Names for the exam: the promisor was William E. Story, the promisee his nephew William E. Story 2d, Sidway was the executor of the uncle's estate, and Louisa Hamer sued as the assignee of the nephew's claim; the case is Hamer v. Sidway, 124 N.Y. 538, 27 N.E. 256 (1891).

Rule in one line: forbearance from a lawful right at the promisor's request is consideration even if the promisor derives no benefit; it is enough that something is promised, done, forborne or suffered by the promisee as consideration for the promise.

sections.Parties: Hamer claimed a right originally held by William E. Story, the nephew, after several assignments. Sidway was executor of the uncle’s estate and resisted payment of the promised $5,000 and interest.
sections.Material Facts:
At a family anniversary celebration in 1869, the uncle promised his nephew $5,000 if the nephew refrained from drinking liquor, using tobacco, swearing, and gambling at cards or billiards for money until age 21. The nephew assented and fully performed the requested restraint. On reaching 21, he notified his uncle.

The uncle acknowledged performance and the debt in a letter, explaining that he would retain the money until he considered the nephew capable of handling it and would pay interest. The nephew agreed to leave it with him. The uncle died without paying the principal. The ultimate plaintiff acquired the claim through intermediate transfers, explaining why neither original contracting party appears in the case name.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court entered judgment for the claimant. The intermediate appellate court reversed. The New York Court of Appeals reversed that order and reinstated the trial-level judgment. An omitted portion, described by the editors, treated the uncle’s later holding of the money as a trust for limitations purposes.
sections.Issue: Was the nephew’s abstention consideration for the uncle’s promise even though it may have improved the nephew’s health and finances and provided no economic benefit to the uncle?
sections.Holding: Yes. The nephew restricted lawful freedom at the uncle’s request in exchange for the promise. That surrendered freedom was a sufficient legal detriment.
sections.Reasoning:
The executor equated detriment with practical harm. The court instead focused on freedom of action. The nephew had a legal right to engage in at least the lawful conduct he abandoned; giving up that right for the promised payment supplied consideration. Courts need not investigate whether the restraint ultimately made his life better or worse, or measure a financial gain to the uncle.

The bargain still matters. The abstention was the performance the uncle requested in return for payment. It was not simply an action taken after learning of an unrelated gift promise. The editors use this distinction to introduce the bargain theory and the difference between an exchange of promises and a promise inviting completed performance. They also emphasize that nominal or sham consideration raises a separate question from whether genuine consideration is economically adequate.

priorVersions.summary: Bargained-for surrender of a legal freedom supplied consideration even though abstention benefited the promisee and brought no financial benefit to the promisor.
priorVersions.notes:
Court: Court of Appeals of New York (1891).

The assignment structure explains why the named plaintiff was not the nephew. Do not confuse this case’s requested abstention with the unrequested retirement in Ricketts or with proof of mere reliance.

sections.Parties: Hamer, the holder of the nephew’s assigned claim, sued Sidway, the executor of the uncle’s estate. The underlying exchange was between William E. Story Sr. and his nephew William E. Story II.
sections.Material Facts: The uncle promised $5,000 if the nephew refrained from specified lawful activities, including drinking, smoking, swearing, and gambling, until age twenty-one. The nephew complied. On reaching twenty-one he wrote to the uncle, who acknowledged the entitlement and proposed to hold the money, with interest, until the nephew could manage it. The claim later passed by assignment.
sections.Procedural History: The Court of Appeals of New York reversed the intermediate court and restored the judgment supporting the claim. Some surrounding trust and limitations questions are omitted from the assigned opinion and are not independently reconstructed.
sections.Issue: Is requested abstention consideration where the promisee gains health or other advantages from it and the promisor receives no economic benefit?
sections.Holding: Yes. The nephew relinquished legal rights at the uncle’s request in exchange for the promise.
sections.Reasoning: The significance of detriment is the surrender of freedom to act, rather than whether the conduct made the nephew poorer or less healthy. Benefit to the promisor is unnecessary where a legally sufficient exchange is present. The notes refine this analysis through the bargain requirement: a merely accidental detriment, personal motive, or recitation of value does not establish that the act and promise were sought and given in exchange. The legal sufficiency of consideration is also distinct from the adequacy of its price.

learning.why: The case explains the legal meaning of detriment and gives a concrete contrast with Ricketts, where quitting work was foreseeable reliance but was not the requested price of the promise.

topics.consideration: Requested forbearance supplies the exchange supporting enforcement.
topics.forbearance: Giving up a lawful choice is a legal detriment even if beneficial.
topics.performance-acceptance: The promise sought actual abstention over the stated period.
topics.assignment: The plaintiff acquired the original promisee’s right through intermediate assignments.
topics.legal-detriment: The holding rests on the nephew's surrender of lawful freedom as a legal detriment, without any benefit to the uncle.
topics.adequacy-consideration: The court refused to ask whether the abstinence actually benefited the uncle or harmed the nephew, illustrating that courts do not weigh the adequacy of consideration.
